Emmeline Pankhurst. The British suffragist and leader of the Women's Social and Political Union, who pioneered militant tactics in the struggle for women's voting rights.

Founded in 1903, the WSPU transformed British suffrage activism from petitions and speeches into direct action. Pankhurst adopted the slogan "Deeds not words." She organized dramatic public demonstrations—heckling politicians, disrupting Parliament, chaining herself to railings. Between 1909 and 1914, she orchestrated campaigns of property destruction. Her members set fires to pillar boxes, broke windows in government buildings, planted bombs—all designed to make suffrage impossible for the government to ignore.

Pankhurst was arrested multiple times. In prison, she endured forced feeding after going on hunger strike, an experience that horrified the public and became a moral rallying point for her cause. The sight of a woman being force-fed in prison transformed public opinion.

When World War One began, she suspended the militant campaign and pivoted the WSPU toward patriotic support for the war effort. This decision proved controversial and fractured the movement. But she lived to see partial victory in 1918, when women over thirty gained the vote, and complete victory in 1928, just before her death. She voted.
